newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Imperial Bank seen buying Oppenheimer.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Imperial Bank seen buying Oppenheimer.

text.p: Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce is set to announce next week that it will acquire mid-sized U.S. brokerage Oppenheimer & Co. for about $500 million, sources close to the deal told Reuters on Thursday.

Insiders said the acquisition of privately owned Oppenheimer, the 12th largest full-service brokerage company in the United States, will give CIBC an immediate strong base in equity underwriting and research and a vast network of institutional sales and trading operations.
Toronto-based CIBC, Canada's second biggest bank, would also gain a comprehensive retail distribution network, asset management and an established mergers and acquisition business.

The sources, who declined to be identified, said CIBC would seek to marry its Canadian leadership in equity underwriting, its position as the number one foreign bank in U.S. loan syndication and strong credit and debt market presence in New York with Oppenheimer's equity strength on Wall Street.
Oppenheimer spokesman John Ryan told Reuters that the investment bank would not comment on the rumors about the deal. CIBC also declined comment.
Founded in 1950, Oppenheimer has assets of $425 million and $11.8 billion worth of assets under management. It has an additional $20 billion of assets in its retail system.

Oppenheimer, ranked 18th in equity underwriting in the United States, did $4.9 billion worth of business in 1996. It has 77 analysts covering 737 companies in eight industries, with 644 retail account executives and 3,022 employees.
Its affiliate Oppenheimer Capital manages more than $54 billion in assets for mutual funds, pensions and wealthy clients.
Analysts said CIBC has made a major commitment to the U.S. market and that the deal would provide it with an attractive vehicle for expansion in North America.

"I think it's obvious that investment banking type operations in the (United) States are important to the bank and they want to expand in those areas," said Kent Wideman, analyst at Dominion Bond Rating Service. "This appears to be something that will fit in nicely."

CIBC would follow rival Canadian banks Toronto-Dominion Bank, which bought U.S. discount broker Waterhouse Investor Services for $519.4 million last October and Bank of Montreal, which purchased Chicago-based retail banker Harris Bank in the 1980s.

Analysts said the high price for Waterhouse could have been a drag on Toronto-Dominion's earnings. But with the strong equity market in North America, the Waterhouse acquisition actually boosted TD's profits.
But analysts noted that the equity market boom was now nine months further along and closer to what they deemed an inevitable downturn.

"I think the risk is that it could be argued that they (CIBC) are buying at the top of the market," said Roy Palmer, analyst at TD Securities Inc. "But unfortunately good firms are not usually for sale when they're cheap."
CIBC shares fell C5 cents to C$37.65 on Thursday on the Toronto Stock Exchange on 1.2 million shares.
Canada's six major banks have grown rapidly outside Canada with the aim of building their operations to prepare for competition with the world's biggest banks.

The large Canadian banks are meanwhile lobbying theCanadian government to allow them to merge with one another before Ottawa contemplates lifting restrictions against foreign banks from competing in Canada's financial services market.

Bank of Nova Scotia and Bank of Montreal now earn more than 40 percent of their profits outside Canada. Scotiabank has been on an acquisition spree and last month made a $908 million bid for National Trustco -- the last big family-owned trust company in Canada.
The same week Royal Bank of Canada launched a $1.7 billion bid for London Insurance Group.
